rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For weak-initial wāw verbs in this class, the verbal noun and place noun take mafʿil, as in al-mawʿid, al-mawḍiʿ, al-mawrid, al-mawjida, and al-mawʿida.
rows.anchor: مفعل وذلك قولك للمكان الموعد والموضع والمورد وفي المصدر الموجدة والموعدة

rows.speaker: أكثر العرب
rows.claim: Most Arabs use muwjil and muwḥil for wajila and waḥila; Sībawayh explains the forms by the verbs’ unstable weak-letter alternations and analogy with other weak forms.
rows.anchor: وقال أكثر العرب في وجل يوجل ووحل يوحل ~~موجل وموحل

rows.speaker: ناس من العرب
rows.claim: Some Arabs preserve the wāw in muwjil and muwḥil, analogizing to verbs such as yarkab after they keep the wāw in yūjil; mawadda likewise keeps its wāw.
rows.anchor: وحدثنا يونس وغيره أن ناسا من العرب يقولون في وجل يوجل ونحوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mawḥid has fatḥa because it is a proper name, not a verbal noun or place noun; it is derived from wāḥid like ʿUmar from ʿĀmir, with parallels such as Mawhib and Mawriq.
rows.anchor: وموحد فتحوه إذ كان اسما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Initial-yāʾ roots behave like sound roots because yāʾ followed by yāʾ is light; maysara is compared with al-maʿjiza, with a reported variant pronunciation of maysara.
rows.anchor: لأنها تتم ولا تعتل وذلك أن الياء مع الياء أخف عليهم ألا تراهم يقولون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The active participle from hollow wāw- and yāʾ-roots has hamza at the medial radical: speakers avoid the original form and cannot use deletion or silence without confusion, yielding khāʾif and bāʾiʿ.
rows.anchor: اعلم أن فاعلا منها مهموز العين وذلك أنهم يكرهون أن يجيء على الأصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive participle follows the defective verb: the medial letter is silenced and the extra wāw drops before another silent letter, giving mazūr and maṣūgh; yāʾ forms similarly give mabyūʿ and mahīb.
rows.anchor: ويعتل مفعول منهما كما اعتل فعل لأن الاسم

rows.speaker: بعض العرب
rows.claim: Some Arabs preserve the original weak radical in makhyūṭ and mabyūʿ, by analogy with ṣayūd and ghayūr; Sībawayh says wāw forms are especially avoided because wāw is heavy with ḍamma.
rows.anchor: وبعض العرب يخرجه على

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The noun pattern mafʿal follows the corresponding defective imperfect, with mīm taking the place of its initial yāʾ, as in maqām, maqāl, mathāba, manāra, al-maghāth, and al-maʿāsh; al-mubayyiḍ and al-musayyir follow the same rule.
rows.anchor: ويجري مفعل مجرى يفعل فيهما فتعتل كما اعتل فعلهما الذي على مثالهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mafʿala forms such as al-maʿūna, al-mashūra, and al-mathūba follow the same pattern; they are not passive participles, since a verbal noun cannot be a passive participle.
rows.anchor: وكذلك مفعلة تجري مجرى يفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For yāʾ-initial roots, mafʿala follows the pattern where the first radical follows the silenced yāʾ, as in maʿīsha; the first radical is not made to follow ḍamma as in the corresponding verb pattern.
rows.anchor: وأما مفعلة من بنات الياء فإنما تجيء على مثال مفعلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some Arabs use the original pattern in the feminine verbal noun, as in al-fukāha la-maqūda ilā al-adhā; Sībawayh says this is irregular, like ajwadt.
rows.anchor: وهذا ليس بمطرد كما أن أجودت ليس بمطرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Name-forming nouns such as makūza, mazīd, and muḥabbab preserve the original pattern as labels, by analogy with names such as Mawriq and Mawhib; this preservation is not a general rule.
rows.anchor: الاسم مشتقا للعلامة لا لمعنى سوى ذا على الأصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Comparative and superlative adjectives from hollow verbs retain the full form, as in aqwal and abyʿ, to distinguish these nouns from inflecting verbs such as aqāla and aqāma; the same applies to mā afʿalahu and afʿil bihi.
rows.anchor: وذلك قولك هو أقول الناس وأبيع الناس وأقول منك وأبيع منك

rows.speaker: بعض العرب
rows.claim: Some speakers hamza the wāw in forms such as adwar, asūq, and athwab because ḍamma over wāw is hard to articulate; yāʾ forms are not hamzaed because ḍamma is lighter there.
rows.anchor: بعض العرب يهمز لوقوع الضمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nominal patterns such as ifʿil and tafaʿʿul are completed in weak roots to distinguish them from finite verbs; examples include iqūl, ibīʿ, taqūla, and tabīʿa.
rows.anchor: وتفعل منهما ليفرق بينهما وبين تفعل وتفعل في الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poetic form tadawwara and the common form al-tatwiba show the completed nominal pattern; Sībawayh cites the poetic line to attest the nominal shape.
rows.anchor: قول العرب في تفعلة من دار يدور تدورة قال الشاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In broken plurals such as maṭiyya/maṭāyā, rakiyya/rakāyā, and hadiyya/hadāyā, the form is faʿāʾil, as in ṣaḥīfa/ṣaḥāʾif.
rows.anchor: وذلك قولك مطية ومطايا وركية وركايا وهدية وهدايا فإنما هذه فعائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The change arises because yāʾ can become alif in mafāʿil and hamza is itself weak; when both weak letters meet in a heavy noun pattern, the yāʾ takes the alif substitution and the hamza is altered.
rows.anchor: مفاعل فتبدل ألفا وذلك نحو مدارى وصحارى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh offers a second account: with alifs on either side, the hamza is like two hamzas; speakers who glottalize salāʾ say salā without glottalization, as if the following hamza triggered the change.
rows.anchor: صارت الهمزة مع الألفين حيث اكتتفتاها بمنزلة همزتين

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say hadāwā, replacing the hamza with wāw because wāw can substitute for hamza.
rows.anchor: قال بعضهم هداوى فأبدلوا الواو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Words whose singular has root wāw, such as idāwa, ʿalāwa, and harāwa, form plurals like harāwā and ʿalāwā, retaining wāw as the yāʾ forms do; this wāw is not the feminine alif.
rows.anchor: وهراوة فإنهم يقولون فيه هراوى وعلاوى وأداوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This substitution is not made in jāʾ because its pattern resembles qāḍ and would be confusable; mafāʿil is not confused with another established pattern.
rows.anchor: هذا في جاء لأنه شيء على مثال قاض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In fawāʿil forms from weak verbs, hamza introduced in the plural remains before yāʾ, as with shawāyā and ḥawāyā; yāʾ and wāw are treated alike in these alternations.
rows.anchor: وفواعل من شويت كذلك لأنها همزة تعرض في الجمع وبعدها الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faʿāʾil from weak roots gives maṭāʾ and ramāʾ because the hamza belongs to the pattern rather than arising in the plural; fiyāʿil yields ḥayāyā and shayāyā by parallel treatment.
rows.anchor: وأما فعائل من بنات الياء والواو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Falwa becomes falāwā because the singular has root wāw, which is represented by wāw in the plural.
rows.anchor: واوا فأبدلوه في الجمع واوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh distinguishes faʿāʾil and fawāʿil from a singular like ḥubārā: because the forms could be confused, he avoids treating them as though they had the same open pattern.
rows.anchor: وأما فعائل وفواعل ففيه مع شبهه بمفاعل

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl gives one parse of this pattern by supplying an omitted second demonstrative or pronoun: the sense is ‘this is travelling’ or ‘he is travelling.’
rows.anchor: وزعم الخليل رحمه الله أن رفعه يكون على وجهين

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl’s second parse makes both following nouns predicates of the demonstrative, like saying ‘this is sweet and sour’ to describe a combined taste.
rows.anchor: الخليل رحمه الله أن رفعه يكون على وجهين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh cites Q 70:15–16, ‘it is a blazing fire, seizing the scalp,’ as a Quranic example in the discussion of raised predicates.
rows.anchor: وقال الله عز وجل @QB@ كلا إنها لظى

rows.speaker: أبي عبد الله
rows.claim: Sībawayh reports Abū ʿAbd Allāh’s reading of the phrase ‘this is my husband, an old man’ as a raised example in the same discussion.
rows.anchor: وزعموا أنها في قراءة أبى عبد الله

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl rejects analyzing al-Akhtal’s fa-abītu lā ḥaraja wa-lā maḥrūm as an ellipsis of anā; that would wrongly license an omitted huwa in ‘kāna ʿAbd Allāh lā muslim wa-lā ṣāliḥ.’
rows.anchor: فزعم الخليل ~~رحمه الله أن هذا ليس

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some instead parse the raised phrase as negation, meaning that the speaker stays blameless and unbereft in the place where he is.
rows.anchor: وقد زعم بعضهم أن رفعه على

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl also explains the wording as an echo of what had been said earlier, like the quoted address ‘O sons of the one whose horns have grown white’; al-Rabīʿ al-Asadī’s verse supports this reported-speech construction.
rows.anchor: وقال الخليل ~~رحمه الله كأنه حكاية لما كان يتكلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh says the alternative explanation based on negation is easier than al-Khalīl’s quotation analysis.
rows.anchor: وقد زعم بعضهم أن رفعه على ~~النفي كأنه قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another raising analysis coordinates ʿAbd Allāh with the demonstrative, yielding ‘ʿAbd Allāh is travelling’; Sībawayh also allows apposition, as in ‘this is Zayd, a travelling man.’
rows.anchor: وقد يكون رفعه على أن تجعل عبد الله معطوفا على هذا كالوصف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh cites ‘by the forelock, a lying forelock’ to show that the second nominative can be apposition (badal) to the first, one of four analyses of the raised construction.
rows.anchor: هذا زيد رجل منطلق على البدل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Majūs and Yahūd are nouns used only for a tribe, with feminine gender prevailing; Imruʾ al-Qays’s simile ‘like the fire of Majūs’ illustrates the usage.
rows.anchor: مجوس ويهود قال امرؤ القيس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Majūs names a man, it is diptote, just like ʿAmmān.
rows.anchor: بمجوس لم تصرفه كما لا تصرفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite forms al-Yahūd and al-Majūs use the article as in nisba adjectives, with the nisba yāʾs deleted; without the article, majūs is indefinite, like majūsiyyīn without its article.
rows.anchor: كما أدخلوها في المجوسي واليهودي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naṣārā is an indefinite plural of naṣrān and naṣrāna; prose normally uses the nisba forms, but the plural omits the nisba yāʾs, like nadāmā from nadmān, and means al-naṣrāniyyīn.
rows.anchor: وأما نصارى فنكرة وإنما نصارى جمع نصران ونصرانة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetry uses naṣārā as an indefinite; a cited line describes the cupbearer of naṣārā, and another poetic example attests the feminine singular naṣrāna.
rows.anchor: ساقي نصارى قبيل الفصح صوام

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl explains tribal plurals in wāw-nūn, such as al-Ashʿarūn and al-Aʿjamūn, as analogical additions alongside broken plurals; the pattern is not productive for every such name.
rows.anchor: سألت الخليل عن قولهم الأشعرون فقال إنما ألحقوا الواو والنون كما كسروا

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl treats maqtawī/maqtawīn like al-Ashʿarī/al-Ashʿarīn.
rows.anchor: وسألوا الخليل عن مقتوي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One possible account of maqtawīn is retention of the original form, parallel to maqātawa; Abū al-Khaṭṭāb reports this word from Arabs, though not all Arabs know it.
rows.anchor: فإن شئت قلت جاءوا به على الأصل كما قالوا مقاتوة حدثنا بذلك أبو الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, maqtawīn may follow madharwīn because it has no singular used independently.
rows.anchor: يكن له واحد يفرد

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl analyzes naṣārā as a plural of naṣrī and naṣrān, like nadmān/nadāmā and mihri/mahārā, with a yāʾ dropped and replaced by alif.
rows.anchor: وأما النصارى فإنه جماع نصري ونصران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh prefers deriving naṣārā from the attested feminine singular naṣrāna, like ashʿath/ashāʿith; he calls this more analogical because naṣrī is unattested.
rows.anchor: هذا قول الخليل وأما الذي نوجهه عليه فأنه جاء على نصرانة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū al-Akhzar al-Ḥammānī’s verse, which explicitly uses naṣrāna, supports Sībawayh’s analysis of naṣārā as a plural of naṣrāna.
rows.anchor: كما سجدت نصرانة لم تحنف
